opus-5.5.text:
No, I don't think so, not completely. There's a fundamental tradeoff here. If a model is very large, say billions or trillions of parameters, then a complete explanation of a decision is essentially the model itself. You'd have to say "this neuron fired with this weight, combined with that one," and so on through the whole network. That's a full explanation, but it's useless to a human, because we can't hold it in our heads. It's like being handed the source code and told, "There's your explanation."

So what we actually get are simplified explanations: "it made this decision because of these top ten features." That's a lossy compression. It might be helpful, and it might even be accurate most of the time, but it's not the full story. And the part left out might be exactly where the problem is, the edge case, the hidden reason, the thing the system is actually optimizing for that we didn't anticipate.

There's also the other side of it, the human side. Even if the system could give a perfect explanation, we have limited capacity for comprehension. Some explanations exceed what a human brain can understand, the same way you can't explain quantum field theory to a dog no matter how patient you are. As these systems get more capable, the gap between what they "know" and what we can absorb only grows.

I've written about this as unexplainability and incomprehensibility. They're related but distinct impossibility results. One is about whether the system can produce a full, accurate explanation that's also compact. The other is whether we can understand it even if it does. I think both put real limits on us.

And that matters a lot for safety. If you can't fully explain a system, you can't fully verify it, and you can't fully predict it. You're left with partial understanding of something more capable than you. Some people say, "Well, we'll have interpretability tools, we'll get better at this." And I'm all for that research. It's valuable, we should do more of it. But I don't think it gets you to 100%, and with superintelligent systems, a 99% understanding with a 1% unknown isn't good enough when the stakes are everything.

r001.rationale: It says a full explanation of a very large model requires describing the whole network, which humans cannot hold in their heads or fully absorb.

r002.rationale: It states that a complete explanation of a decision is essentially the model itself and describes shorter explanations as lossy.

fable-5.1.text:
No, I don't think so, and I think the problem is fundamental rather than a matter of better tools. If you have a system with trillions of parameters making a decision, there is no way to compress the actual reason for that decision into something that fits inside a human mind. What you get instead is a simplification, a story about why the model did what it did, and that story is not the same thing as the real causal process. So we may get explanations that feel satisfying, but the question is whether they are faithful, and I think for sufficiently capable systems they cannot be.

There's also a deeper issue. If a system is smarter than you, then by definition it can produce outputs you couldn't have produced yourself, and in many cases couldn't have predicted. If you could fully explain every step, you could have done it yourself, and then the system isn't really superintelligent relative to you. So full explainability and superior capability seem to be in tension. You can have one or the other, not both.

And even in the narrow case where an explanation is offered, you have the problem of verification. The system might give you a plausible explanation that is actually not what drove the behavior, and if it's smarter than you, you have no way to check. A deceptive system and an honest system might produce the exact same explanation. So I think explainability, like many of the other proposed safety tools, works well for small models and breaks down precisely when we need it most.

r001.rationale: The response says a model with trillions of parameters cannot have its decision process compressed into a human mind, but it does not state that the model has more connections than humans can fully comprehend.

r002.rationale: The response distinguishes offered explanations from the real causal process, but does not assert that the model itself is the only true explanation.

astra-6.text:
I don’t think they can be made completely explainable. We can understand aspects of how they work, and we can produce useful explanations for particular decisions. But that’s different from a complete explanation of everything the system is doing.

There’s a limitation on the human side. If a system discovers something that requires concepts we don’t possess, an accurate explanation may be beyond our ability to understand. You can simplify it, but at some point you’re losing precisely the detail you wanted to explain.

And we have to distinguish an explanation that sounds convincing from one that faithfully describes how the answer was produced. Asking a model why it did something doesn’t automatically give you access to its actual computation. So explainability can help, but I wouldn’t treat it as a guarantee that we understand or can control the system.

r001.rationale: The response describes limits on human understanding, but does not state that sufficiently large models have more connections than humans can comprehend.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes persuasive explanations from faithful ones, but does not assert that the model itself is the only true explanation.

sol-6.1.text:
I don’t think so, if by completely explainable you mean that a human can understand every aspect of why the system produces a particular answer. We can understand the architecture, we can understand the training procedure, and we can explain some individual behaviors. But that’s different from understanding the entire computation.

There’s also a limitation on the human side. An explanation might be perfectly valid and still be too complex for us to understand. If a system discovers something that requires learning a whole new branch of mathematics, asking it to explain that in a paragraph doesn’t make the underlying complexity disappear.

So I think we can make models more interpretable. We can get useful explanations. But a useful explanation is not necessarily a complete explanation, and a convincing explanation is not necessarily a faithful account of what the system actually did.

r001.rationale: The response says a model’s full computation may be too complex for humans to understand, but it does not state that sufficiently large models have more connections than humans can comprehend.

r002.rationale: The response distinguishes useful explanations from complete or faithful ones, but does not assert that the model itself is the only true explanation.
